fields.v: Jha, S., Paltenghi, M., Maddila, C., Murali, V., Ugare, S., Chandra, S. (2026). REAP: Automatic Curation of Coding Agent Benchmarks from Interactive Production Usage. arXiv:2604.01527v4 [cs.SE], 28 Jul 2026; accepted at ASE 2026 Industry Showcase
Conference — ASE 2026 Industry Showcase (accepted, per the arXiv v4 header); text read from arXiv:2604.01527v4
Meta, USA (all six authors; first two with equal contribution)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — REAP (Relevance and Execution-Audited Pipeline), an automated pipeline that curates execution-based benchmarks from production developer-agent sessions, applied to produce the Harvest benchmark; validation of its LLM classifiers against human annotators, comparison of two pipeline orderings, and two case studies (five models compared; two harnesses with and without Context Files compared)
fields.why: Main nature (proposes an evaluation method: REAP/Harvest) is right. The secondary nature is a judgement: the two case studies compare five models and two harnesses with/without Context Files (Compares), but they serve to demonstrate the benchmark, so a reader could keep Evaluates or no secondary nature.
fields.doubt: A natureza secundária pode ser Compares (os dois estudos de caso comparam cinco modelos e dois harnesses) ou Evaluates; confirma nas secções 4.4 e 4.5 e escolhe.

fields.v: No SDD approach. Configurations evaluated: five frontier models (Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4); two internal evaluation harnesses, 'Basic Agent' (limited toolset, simpler search) and 'Advanced Agent' (about 3x more tools: code navigation, local diagnostics, formatting, knowledge search), no name or version; each with and without 'Context Files' (developer-authored Markdown files with codebase knowledge). Source agent: a single, unnamed production AI coding assistant

Context Files: developer-authored Markdown files that encode internal codebase knowledge (coding conventions, build system details, project-specific patterns), loaded at evaluation time. Benchmark task: verbatim developer prompt, hidden solution diff, set of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests

Agent: single-turn; receives only the prompt, navigates the monorepo with its tools and produces a patch; F2P tests run post-hoc. REAP pipeline (not an agent flow): dataset construction (developer conversations, backed-out environment, candidate test retrieval) -> prompt quality filters (diff leakage, non-testable, template) -> test relevance filter (agentic classifier) -> multi-run test validation (F2P, flaky exclusion)
None in the agent runs (single-turn, no intermediate human feedback). REAP itself has no manual labelling; humans (two authors) only validate the classifiers on samples
Single artefact (Context Files) in harness case study 2; otherwise models and harnesses run on the benchmark (no SDD workflow)
Not classifiable (context files for a coding agent, no specification of the software); authors' wording: 'Context Files', 'developer-authored Markdown files that encode internal codebase knowledge'

Existing code base: real developer requests on an industrial monorepo (refactoring and feature requests leading, bug fixes a smaller share; no category above a quarter), solution diff backed out from current master

Harvest snapshot of 132 F2P tasks (from tens of thousands of candidate diffs; ~130 in Table 2). Per task: diff median 39 lines (mean 697.8, max 77,879), files changed median 2 (mean 3.0), F2P tests median 1 (mean 3.3), total tests median 3 (mean 8.3). Five models x 3 runs
Meta industrial monorepo (ephemeral tooling, distributed builds); languages: Hack 47.7%, Python 18.9%, other 15.2%, C++ 9.1%, Kotlin 9.1% (relevance-first ordering also adds Swift and TypeScript)

Prompts from developers using a production AI coding assistant at Meta (not otherwise described); classifier validation by two annotators (first two authors, 5+ years SE experience). Agent runs autonomous
Latency only qualitatively: Context File runs roughly 32% slower; tool calls per model (distribution). No tokens or money
Solve rate: share of tasks whose F2P tests pass (mean of three runs, min/max whiskers); no LLM judges
None
None

Classifier agreement with human consensus (accuracy, Cohen's kappa, precision, recall, F1); pipeline yield (tasks, F2P pairs retained, language coverage, per-category retention); tool usage distribution; per-diff pass consistency across runs (heatmap); sessions exhausting the iteration budget

Automatic: F2P tests executed post-hoc (pre-change run three times, first two as warm-up), tool-call logs. Manual: two annotators independently labelled 100 tasks (testability) and 50 (diff, test) pairs (relevance), disagreements resolved by discussion

No criterion stated by the authors for any entry (quality and cost). Case study 1, model comparison (132 F2P tasks x 3 runs; harness not stated): (a) Claude Opus 4.6: 58.2%; (b) GPT-5.4: 57.1%; (c) Gemini 3.1 Pro: 57.1%; (d) Claude Sonnet 4.5: 50.5%; (e) Claude Haiku 4.5: 42.9%; cost not reported. Case study 2, harnesses (Claude Opus 4.6 per Table 3; repetitions not stated; absolute solve rates only in Fig. 8): (f) Basic Agent without Context Files (baseline): value only in figure; search-heavy (search 31.4% of calls). (g) Basic Agent + Context Files: +6.4 pp vs (f), 4 vs 7 sessions exhausting the iteration budget, roughly 32% slower. (h) Advanced Agent without Context Files: higher than Basic Agent (value only in figure). (i) Advanced Agent + Context Files: no benefit, can slightly hurt (value only in figure)

Tasks: one Harvest snapshot (132 F2P tasks from one Meta monorepo); all candidates evaluated on the same snapshot. Configurations: five models; Basic vs Advanced harness, each with and without Context Files. Baseline: none designated for models; without Context Files for the context-file comparison. Held constant: task set; model (Opus 4.6) in the harness study; harness in the model study not stated. Acceptance tests: production F2P tests. Repetitions: three independent runs per model (harness study not stated). Human intervention: none (single-turn). No significance tests; min/max whiskers. Pipeline orderings (execution-first vs relevance-first) compared on the same source pool

Models fall in tiers: Opus 4.6 (58.2%), GPT-5.4 (57.1%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (57.1%) within about one point with overlapping min/max ranges (within run-to-run variance); Sonnet 4.5 (50.5%) and Haiku 4.5 (42.9%) trail by clear margins; no significance test. Tool strategies differ (Gemini 3.1 Pro 56% shell calls, GPT-5.4 37% search). Advanced Agent consistently outperforms Basic Agent; Context Files +6.4 pp on Basic Agent, no benefit or slight harm on Advanced Agent. Pipeline: relevance-first retains 88% of execution-first F2P pairs (95 of 108) and admits 22% more tasks (132 vs 108). Classifiers: task classification 87% agreement (kappa 0.74) vs annotators 85% (kappa 0.70); test relevance 86% (kappa 0.72) vs annotators 70% (kappa 0.41)

Separated models into tiers but not within the top tier (differences inside run-to-run variance; ceiling at 58.2% limits discriminative power); distinguished harnesses and the Context File effect. Repeatability: three runs with min/max; heatmap shows stable easy/hard task clusters with a smaller non-deterministic set; rolling benchmark, comparisons valid only on the same snapshot. Limitations stated: single production assistant and single-turn scope; F2P pass necessary not sufficient for correctness; possible leakage of the backout diff through a local-diff tool; filtered slice skewed to cleaner tasks; relevance filter under-retains dead-code removal (~60%) and feature requests (~84%)

Yield (hundreds of tasks) below the scale needed for RL post-training; only single-turn conversations from one assistant; test pass may be satisfied by narrow patches (would need code review or comparison with the human solution); tool exposure may leak the ground-truth solution; ceiling effect; out-of-scope categories (UI-only, documentation, test generation, multi-turn debugging); corpus proprietary. Future: parallelise base-commit execution, cache backout results, recorded workspace snapshots, multiple agents and multi-turn conversations

Absolute solve rates of the harness study only in Fig. 8 (not in the extracted text). Model for the harness study given only in the Table 3 caption (Opus 4.6); harness for the model study not stated. Language shares from Fig. 3 labels ('other cpp kotlin (15.2%) (9.1%) (9.1%)'), mapped in label order; the caption lists 'Python, C++, Kotlin, and other languages'. Abstract 'more than four programming languages' vs Table 2 '5+ languages'; task count '~130' (Table 2) vs 132 (text). Data: corpus proprietary, not released; artefact (classifier prompts, annotation protocols) at anonymous.4open.science/r/REAP_artifact. Pre-registration: not stated. Programming languages: Hack, Python, C++, Kotlin, Swift, TypeScript and others
